_note: Year 3 English Term 4 (end-of-year consolidation) item bank: 16 skills x 10 items covering handwriting, multimodal texts, spelling, imaginative writing, grammar, fluent reading, oral presentation, comprehension, editing, text analysis, descriptive language, reflective writing, text structure, language choices, the publishing process, and a year-end review.

items.questionText: What does it mean for handwriting to be 'legible'? A) written very quickly   B) easy for someone else to read   C) written only in capital letters
items.answerKey: easy for someone else to read
stepByStepSolution: Think about what the word 'legible' is used to describe.
Legible writing is writing that can be read without difficulty.
So legible handwriting means it is clear and easy to read.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking 'legible' means 'fast' rather than 'readable'.
Thinking legible writing must be joined-up (cursive) to count.
hints: Think about what a reader needs to be able to do with your writing.
The word starts the same as 'legibility' — it's all about being able to read something clearly.

items.questionText: Which feature helps handwriting stay consistent and easy to read? A) making every letter a different size   B) keeping letters a similar size and sitting on the line   C) squeezing letters close together with no gaps
items.answerKey: keeping letters a similar size and sitting on the line
stepByStepSolution: Consistent handwriting means the letters look similar to each other.
Letters that are all a similar height and sit neatly on the line are easier to read.
Random sizes and squashed letters make writing harder to follow.
commonMisconceptions: Believing bigger letters are always better.
Thinking consistency doesn't matter as long as letters are neat individually.
hints: Picture two pieces of writing — one where every letter is a different size, and one where they're even.
The answer is about letters being the same height and sitting on the line.

items.questionText: Why do we leave a small space between each word when we write?
answerKey: so the reader can tell where one word ends and the next begins
to make it clear where words start and stop
stepByStepSolution: Think about what happens if words are squashed together with no space.
Without spaces, words can run into each other and become hard to separate.
A small gap shows the reader exactly where one word finishes and the next begins.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking spacing is just about making writing look neat, not about making meaning clear.
Leaving no space or leaving huge gaps between words.
hints: Imagine reading a sentence with no gaps between the words at all.
The answer is about helping the reader know where each word starts and ends.

items.questionText: Sam's handwriting has letters that lean in different directions and change size from tiny to huge within the same sentence. What is one change Sam could make to improve legibility?
answerKey: make the letters a more consistent size
keep the letters the same size and slant
stepByStepSolution: Look at what is making Sam's writing hard to read.
Uneven size and slant make it difficult for a reader's eye to follow the words smoothly.
Practising keeping letters a similar size and slant will make his writing more legible.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking speed is the main problem rather than consistency.
Suggesting Sam should just write in capitals instead of fixing size and slant.
hints: Think about what 'consistent' handwriting looks like.
Focus your answer on letter size and slant being more even.

items.questionText: Which description best matches legible handwriting? A) letters of different heights, overlapping, with no gaps between words   B) letters sitting evenly on the line, similar in size, with clear spaces between words   C) letters written extremely small so more fits on the page
items.answerKey: letters sitting evenly on the line, similar in size, with clear spaces between words
stepByStepSolution: Compare the three descriptions to see which features help a reader.
Even letter height, sitting on the line, and clear spacing all support easy reading.
Overlapping letters or letters that are too tiny to read clearly make writing hard to follow.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking smaller writing is automatically neater.
Overlooking spacing as part of legibility and only thinking about letter shape.
hints: Rule out the option where letters overlap with no gaps.
The correct answer mentions three things: even size, sitting on the line, and spacing.

items.questionText: What is 'letter formation'?
answerKey: the way each letter is shaped or written
how you form the shape of each letter, e.g. where you start and which way you move your pencil
stepByStepSolution: Break down the phrase: 'letter' and 'formation'.
'Formation' relates to how something is built or shaped.
So letter formation means the way each letter's shape is built, stroke by stroke.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing letter formation with letter size.
Thinking it only matters for cursive writing, not printing.
hints: Think about the individual strokes used to make a letter, like 'a' or 'b'.
The answer describes how the shape of a letter is made.

items.questionText: A student writes the letters 'b' and 'd' the same way, which confuses readers. This is mostly a problem with: A) letter spacing   B) letter formation   C) page layout
items.answerKey: letter formation
stepByStepSolution: Think about what 'b' and 'd' have in common and what makes them different.
'b' and 'd' are mirror images — they need to be formed with the loop on the correct side.
Mixing up how each letter is shaped is a letter formation issue, not a spacing or layout issue.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking this is a spacing problem because the letters look similar.
Believing letter reversals are only about page layout.
hints: Think about which part of handwriting decides the shape of each letter.
The issue is about how the letter itself is drawn, not the space around it.

items.questionText: Explain one reason a teacher might ask you to check your letter formation, even when your handwriting already looks fairly neat.
answerKey: so your writing stays consistent and easy to read as you write faster
correct formation helps your handwriting stay clear even when you write quickly, and stops bad habits forming
stepByStepSolution: Think about handwriting over a long time, not just one piece of work.
If letters are formed correctly, writing usually stays legible even when done quickly.
Checking formation early helps prevent habits that could make writing messier later.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking that neat-looking writing means the formation must already be correct.
Believing formation only matters for beginners, not for building good long-term habits.
hints: Think about what happens to handwriting when someone writes very quickly, like in a test.
The answer is about writing staying legible even under time pressure, and avoiding habits that cause problems later.

items.questionText: Which of these is the best reason for using lined paper when practising handwriting? A) it makes writing look more colourful   B) it helps letters sit evenly and stay a consistent size   C) it lets you write faster
items.answerKey: it helps letters sit evenly and stay a consistent size
stepByStepSolution: Think about what lines on paper are designed to do.
Lines give a guide for where letters should sit and how tall they should be.
This supports consistent size and even placement, which are features of legible handwriting.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking lined paper is only about neatness, not about consistent size and placement.
Believing lines are mainly about speed rather than guiding letter shape and size.
hints: Think about what a line on the page actually guides you to do.
The best answer links lines to keeping letters even and a consistent size.

items.questionText: Name two features you would check when proofreading your own handwriting for legibility.
answerKey: letter size and spacing
letter formation and consistent size
spacing between words and consistent letter size
stepByStepSolution: Think back to the features of legible handwriting: size, spacing, formation, and sitting on the line.
Choose two of these features that a writer could check by looking back over their own work.
Two reasonable answers are checking letter size/consistency and checking spacing between words.
commonMisconceptions: Only checking spelling instead of handwriting features.
Thinking proofreading handwriting means checking punctuation, not the shape and spacing of letters.
hints: Think about the list of features that make handwriting legible: size, spacing, formation, sitting on the line.
Pick any two of those features for your answer.

items.questionText: What is a 'multimodal text'? A) a text written only in one language   B) a text that combines two or more modes, like words, images, and sound   C) a text that is very long
items.answerKey: a text that combines two or more modes, like words, images, and sound
stepByStepSolution: Break down 'multi' (many) and 'modal' (modes, or ways of communicating).
A multimodal text uses more than one way of communicating meaning.
Examples include a slideshow with pictures and captions, or a video with narration and music.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking multimodal just means 'multimedia' with no connection to combining meaning.
Believing any long text automatically counts as multimodal.
hints: Think about the word parts: multi- and modal.
The answer mentions combining more than one mode, like words and images.

items.questionText: Which of these is an example of a real audience for a multimodal project? A) nobody, because it's just for practice   B) your class, family, or school community who will actually see it   C) an audience that doesn't exist
items.answerKey: your class, family, or school community who will actually see it
stepByStepSolution: Think about who a 'real audience' could be, compared to an imaginary one.
A real audience is made up of actual people who will view or use your finished text.
Your classmates, teacher, family or school community are all examples of a real audience.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking 'real audience' has to mean strangers on the internet.
Believing an audience must be very large to count as 'real'.
hints: Think about people who could genuinely look at your finished project.
The answer includes people close to you, like classmates or family.

items.questionText: Name one mode (way of communicating) you could include in a multimodal text, other than written words.
answerKey: images
pictures
sound
music
video
narration
diagrams
stepByStepSolution: Think about ways people communicate ideas besides writing.
Pictures, diagrams, sound, and video are all different modes.
Choosing modes that suit your purpose makes your multimodal text stronger.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking 'mode' only refers to written text.
Believing you must use every possible mode in one project.
hints: Think about what you might add to a slideshow besides text.
Any answer like images, sound, or video works.

items.questionText: Before creating a multimodal project, why is it important to plan your purpose and audience first?
answerKey: so you choose the right content, modes and language for the people who will see it
planning purpose and audience helps you decide what to include and how to present it
stepByStepSolution: Think about how a project for younger students might differ from one for adults.
Your purpose (to inform, persuade or entertain) affects what content you choose.
Your audience affects the language, images and modes that will work best.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking planning is only about deciding the topic, not the audience.
Believing purpose and audience don't affect the final choices in a project.
hints: Think about how you'd change a project if it were for a completely different audience.
The answer connects planning to choosing suitable content and modes.

items.questionText: Which step comes first when creating a multimodal text independently? A) publishing the finished project   B) planning the purpose, audience and content   C) editing the final draft
items.answerKey: planning the purpose, audience and content
stepByStepSolution: Think about the writing process in order: plan, create, edit, publish.
Planning always comes first, before creating or editing.
Publishing is the very last step, once everything else is finished.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking editing happens before creating any content.
Believing you can publish before planning what the text is for.
hints: Think about the general order of the writing process.
The first step is always about deciding purpose, audience and content.

items.questionText: Which is the best reason to choose an image to go with a paragraph of text? A) it fills up empty space on the page   B) it supports and adds meaning to what the words say   C) it makes the project longer
items.answerKey: it supports and adds meaning to what the words say
stepByStepSolution: Think about why creators combine images with words in the first place.
A well-chosen image should add information or help explain the words.
Images used only to fill space don't add real meaning to the text.
commonMisconceptions: Believing any image is fine as long as it looks nice.
Thinking images are just decoration rather than adding meaning.
hints: Think about what makes an image actually useful in a project, not just decorative.
The best answer links the image to supporting the words' meaning.

items.questionText: What does it mean to 'publish' a multimodal project?
answerKey: to share the finished version with an audience
to make the final version available for others to see
stepByStepSolution: Think about the last step of the writing process.
Publishing means the project is finished and ready to be shared.
This could mean presenting it to the class, printing it, or posting it online.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking publishing only means putting something on the internet.
Confusing publishing with editing, which happens before the final version.
hints: Think about what happens once a project is completely finished.
The answer is about sharing the final version with others.

items.questionText: You are creating a multimodal project to persuade your school to start a recycling program. Which mode would most strongly support your persuasive point about how much rubbish the school produces? A) a graph showing how much rubbish the school throws away each week   B) a random drawing of a cartoon animal   C) changing the text to a fancy font
items.answerKey: a graph showing how much rubbish the school throws away each week
stepByStepSolution: Think about your purpose: persuading people using evidence.
A graph presents real data that supports your argument clearly.
A random drawing or fancy font doesn't add evidence to support persuasion.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any visual addition automatically strengthens persuasion.
Believing decoration is as powerful as evidence when persuading.
hints: Think about what kind of mode provides real evidence, not just decoration.
The best answer is the one showing actual data.

items.questionText: Which best describes 'creating independently' when making a multimodal text? A) a partner does all the planning and you just present it   B) you take responsibility for planning, making choices, and completing most of the work yourself   C) the teacher tells you exactly what to write and you copy it
items.answerKey: you take responsibility for planning, making choices, and completing most of the work yourself
stepByStepSolution: Think about what 'independently' means in general.
Working independently means making your own decisions and doing the work yourself.
This doesn't mean no help at all, but you are responsible for the main choices and effort.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking independent work means getting no help or feedback at all.
Confusing independent work with simply following exact instructions from someone else.
hints: Think about the everyday meaning of 'independent'.
The answer is about taking responsibility for your own choices and work.

items.questionText: After publishing a multimodal project, why might it be useful to ask your audience for feedback?
answerKey: to find out what worked well and what could be improved next time
feedback helps you understand if your purpose was achieved and how to improve future projects
stepByStepSolution: Think about the purpose of your project — was it to inform, persuade or entertain?
Feedback from your audience tells you whether your project achieved that purpose.
This information can help you improve your next multimodal project.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking feedback is only useful before publishing, not after.
Believing feedback is only about pointing out mistakes rather than what worked well too.
hints: Think about how you would know if your project actually worked for its audience.
The answer connects feedback to understanding success and planning improvements.

items.questionText: Which spelling strategy uses knowing what a word 'looks like' to check if it's spelled correctly? A) visual strategy   B) phonic strategy   C) morphemic strategy
items.answerKey: visual strategy
stepByStepSolution: Think about the meaning of 'visual' — related to sight.
A visual strategy means picturing or checking how a word usually looks.
This is different from sounding a word out (phonic) or breaking it into meaningful parts (morphemic).
commonMisconceptions: Confusing visual strategies with sounding words out.
Thinking all spelling strategies are the same thing.
hints: Think about the word 'visual' and what it relates to.
The answer is about how a word looks, not how it sounds.

items.questionText: Which spelling strategy involves listening to the sounds in a word and matching them to letters? A) morphemic strategy   B) phonic strategy   C) visual strategy
items.answerKey: phonic strategy
stepByStepSolution: Think about the word 'phonic', which relates to sound.
A phonic strategy breaks a word into its sounds and matches each sound to letters.
This helps spell words that follow regular sound patterns.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking phonic strategies only apply to short words.
Confusing phonic strategy with checking how a word looks.
hints: Think about the root of the word 'phonic'.
The answer relates to sounding out a word.

items.questionText: What is a 'prefix'?
answerKey: a word part added to the beginning of a word that changes its meaning
letters added before a base word to change its meaning
stepByStepSolution: Think about the word parts 'pre' (before) and 'fix' (attach).
A prefix is attached to the beginning of a base word.
Adding a prefix, like 'un' in 'unhappy', changes the word's meaning.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing prefixes with suffixes, which go at the end of a word.
Thinking a prefix is a whole separate word rather than a word part.
hints: Think about where 'pre' usually appears in a word — at the start or the end?
The answer describes a word part added before a base word.

items.questionText: The word 'unhappily' can be broken into three word parts. Name them.
answerKey: un, happy, ly
un-happy-ly
stepByStepSolution: Look for a prefix at the start of the word.
'Un' is the prefix, 'happy' is the base word, and 'ly' is the suffix.
Breaking a word into its parts (morphemes) can help you spell longer words correctly.
commonMisconceptions: Missing the spelling change from 'happy' to 'happi' before adding 'ly'.
Forgetting that both a prefix and a suffix can appear in the same word.
hints: Look for a word part at the beginning and a word part at the end.
The three parts are 'un', 'happy', and 'ly'.

items.questionText: Which strategy would help you remember that 'said' is not spelled the way it sounds? A) phonic strategy   B) visual strategy (remembering how it looks)   C) morphemic strategy
items.answerKey: visual strategy (remembering how it looks)
stepByStepSolution: Think about whether 'said' follows regular sound-to-letter rules.
'Said' is spelled in an unusual way that doesn't match its sound closely.
Remembering how tricky words look on the page (a visual strategy) works better than sounding them out.
commonMisconceptions: Trying to sound out tricky words exactly as they're pronounced.
Thinking every word can be spelled correctly using only phonics.
hints: Think about whether this word sounds the way it's spelled.
For tricky words, a visual strategy usually works best.

items.questionText: What spelling strategy could help you spell the word 'unfair' correctly if you already know how to spell 'fair'?
answerKey: morphemic strategy (recognising the base word 'fair' and adding the prefix 'un')
breaking the word into the prefix 'un' and the base word 'fair'
stepByStepSolution: Notice that 'unfair' contains the smaller word 'fair'.
Recognising the base word and adding the prefix 'un' is a morphemic strategy.
This strategy uses your knowledge of word parts and their meanings to spell new words.
commonMisconceptions: Trying to sound out the whole word instead of noticing the base word.
Not recognising that 'un' changes the meaning to the opposite.
hints: Look for a smaller, familiar word hiding inside 'unfair'.
The strategy is about recognising word parts, called morphemic knowledge.

items.questionText: Which word uses the suffix '-ful' correctly? A) hopefull   B) hopeful   C) hopfull
items.answerKey: hopeful
stepByStepSolution: Remember that the suffix '-ful' only has one 'l', even though 'full' has two.
Check the base word 'hope' keeps its spelling before adding the suffix.
Putting them together correctly gives 'hopeful'.
commonMisconceptions: Adding an extra 'l' because the suffix sounds like the word 'full'.
Dropping the 'e' from 'hope' when it isn't needed before '-ful'.
hints: Remember the suffix '-ful' has only one 'l'.
Combine 'hope' and 'ful' without doubling any letters.

items.questionText: Explain how knowing the meaning of the prefix 're-' can help you spell and understand the word 'rewrite'.
answerKey: 're-' means 'again', so 'rewrite' means to write again, which helps you spell and understand the word
knowing 're-' means again helps you build and understand the word 'rewrite' as 're' plus 'write'
stepByStepSolution: Recall that the prefix 're-' means 'again' or 'back'.
Adding 're-' to 'write' creates a new word meaning 'write again'.
Knowing the prefix's meaning helps you both spell the word correctly and understand what it means.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking prefixes only affect spelling, not meaning.
Not recognising 'write' as the base word inside 'rewrite'.
hints: Think about what 're-' usually means in other words, like 'redo' or 'replay'.
Connect the meaning of 're-' to writing something again.

items.questionText: Which sentence shows the best use of a spelling strategy to check an unfamiliar word? A) guessing the spelling and moving on without checking   B) breaking the word into sounds or parts, then checking if it looks right   C) copying the word from a friend without checking it makes sense
items.answerKey: breaking the word into sounds or parts, then checking if it looks right
stepByStepSolution: Think about what good spellers do when they meet an unfamiliar word.
Good spellers often try more than one strategy — sounding it out, breaking it into parts, and checking how it looks.
Guessing without checking, or copying without understanding, are not reliable strategies.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking guessing is an acceptable spelling strategy.
Believing copying a word means you understand how to spell it.
hints: Think about combining more than one strategy to check a word.
The best answer involves both trying the word and checking it looks correct.

items.questionText: A student spells 'because' as 'bcos'. Which spelling strategy would help fix this, and why?
answerKey: a visual strategy, because 'because' is a tricky word that doesn't match its sounds closely
visual strategy — remembering how the word looks, since sounding it out alone won't give the correct spelling
stepByStepSolution: Notice that 'bcos' matches the sounds of 'because' but not its actual spelling.
This shows that phonic strategies alone aren't enough for tricky, irregular words.
A visual strategy — remembering how the word looks — is better suited to spelling 'because' correctly.
commonMisconceptions: Continuing to rely only on sounding the word out.
Assuming all spelling mistakes are because a student doesn't know the word's meaning.
hints: Think about why sounding the word out led to this mistake.
The strategy that helps is about remembering what the word looks like.

items.questionText: When planning an imaginative story, which of these should you decide on first? A) the exact spelling of every word   B) your character, setting and basic plot idea   C) how neat your handwriting will be
items.answerKey: your character, setting and basic plot idea
stepByStepSolution: Think about what a story needs before you start writing sentences.
Planning helps you decide who the story is about (character), where it happens (setting), and what happens (plot).
Spelling and handwriting are checked later, during editing, not during initial planning.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking spelling and handwriting come before planning ideas.
Believing you can start writing without any plan at all.
hints: Think about the big picture of a story before the small details.
The answer includes character, setting and plot idea.

items.questionText: What is a 'literary device'?
answerKey: a technique writers use to create an effect, like a simile or metaphor
a special technique authors use to make their writing more interesting, such as a simile
stepByStepSolution: Think about the word 'device', which means a tool or technique.
In writing, a literary device is a special technique used to create an effect.
Examples include similes, metaphors, and onomatopoeia.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a literary device is the same as a full sentence or paragraph.
Believing literary devices are only used in poetry.
hints: Think of it as a writing 'tool' authors use on purpose.
Give an example type, like a simile, in your answer if it helps.

items.questionText: Which sentence includes a simile? A) The dog ran fast down the street.   B) The dog ran like lightning down the street.   C) The dog ran down the street and barked.
items.answerKey: The dog ran like lightning down the street.
stepByStepSolution: Remember that a simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as'.
Look for the word 'like' or 'as' connecting two different things.
'Ran like lightning' compares the dog's speed to lightning, so it is a simile.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any exciting sentence must contain a simile.
Missing the comparison word 'like' or 'as' as the key clue.
hints: Look for the word 'like' or 'as' in the sentence.
The simile compares the dog's running to something else.

items.questionText: Name two things a writer should think about when developing a character for an imaginative story.
answerKey: the character's personality and appearance
how the character feels and behaves, and what they look like
the character's traits and what they want
stepByStepSolution: Think about what makes a character feel real to a reader.
Writers often consider a character's appearance, personality, feelings, and goals.
Choosing two of these details, such as personality and appearance, helps develop a believable character.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a character only needs a name to be developed.
Focusing only on what a character looks like and ignoring their personality or feelings.
hints: Think about what you'd want to know about a new character in a book.
Two good answers are personality and appearance, or feelings and goals.

items.questionText: Which sentence best establishes a spooky setting? A) It was a sunny day at the beach.   B) The abandoned house creaked in the cold, silent night.   C) Maya ate breakfast before school.
items.answerKey: The abandoned house creaked in the cold, silent night.
stepByStepSolution: Think about which words create a mood in each sentence.
Words like 'abandoned', 'creaked', 'cold' and 'silent night' create a spooky, tense feeling.
The other sentences describe ordinary, everyday events without a spooky mood.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any sentence with a setting automatically creates a strong mood.
Overlooking specific mood words as the key to atmosphere.
hints: Look for words that create a tense or eerie feeling.
The correct sentence mentions an abandoned house and a silent night.

items.questionText: During editing, why might a writer change some of their vocabulary choices in an imaginative story?
answerKey: to make the writing more vivid, precise or interesting for the reader
to choose stronger or more descriptive words that improve the story
stepByStepSolution: Think about what editing is for — improving a draft, not just fixing errors.
Writers often replace plain words with more vivid or precise ones during editing.
This makes descriptions of characters and settings more engaging for the reader.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking editing is only about fixing spelling and punctuation.
Believing the first word choice is always the best one.
hints: Think about the difference between a first draft and a polished final version.
The answer is about making word choices more vivid or interesting.

items.questionText: Which of these is an example of onomatopoeia? A) The thunder rumbled and crashed.   B) The thunder was very loud.   C) The thunder happened during the storm.
items.answerKey: The thunder rumbled and crashed.
stepByStepSolution: Remember that onomatopoeia uses words that imitate sounds.
'Rumbled' and 'crashed' sound like the noises they describe.
The other sentences describe the thunder without using sound-imitating words.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any word about sound counts as onomatopoeia.
Confusing onomatopoeia with simply describing volume, like 'loud'.
hints: Look for words that sound like the noise they describe.
'Rumbled' and 'crashed' are the clue words.

items.questionText: Explain why planning a story's ending before you start drafting can make an imaginative story stronger.
answerKey: it helps the events and clues in the story lead logically towards that ending
knowing the ending helps you plan events that build towards it, making the story more connected
stepByStepSolution: Think about stories that feel disconnected compared to ones that feel well planned.
When a writer knows the ending, they can plan events and details that build towards it.
This makes the whole story feel connected and purposeful, rather than random.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking planning the ending limits creativity rather than supporting it.
Believing a story can only be improved during editing, not during planning.
hints: Think about how knowing where a story is going affects the choices you make earlier.
The answer connects planning the ending to a more connected, logical story.

items.questionText: A student's draft says: 'The dragon was scary. It had big teeth. It roared loudly.' Which revision best improves this using a literary device? A) The dragon was very very scary and had really big teeth.   B) The dragon's roar was like rolling thunder, and its teeth glinted like knives.   C) The dragon was scary and had teeth and roared.
items.answerKey: The dragon's roar was like rolling thunder, and its teeth glinted like knives.
stepByStepSolution: Compare the three revisions for vivid, descriptive language.
Option B uses similes ('like rolling thunder', 'like knives') to create strong images.
The other options either repeat weak words or don't add any descriptive technique.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking adding more plain adjectives (like 'very very scary') is the same as using a literary device.
Not recognising similes as a way to improve description.
hints: Look for comparisons using 'like' or 'as' in the revisions.
The strongest revision uses two similes.

items.questionText: Name one question you could ask yourself when editing your imaginative story to check your character is well developed.
answerKey: does the character's actions match their personality?
would the reader understand how the character feels and why they act that way?
have I shown the character's personality through what they say and do?
stepByStepSolution: Think about what makes a character feel believable to a reader.
A good editing question checks whether the character's actions, feelings and personality fit together.
Asking this helps you notice if more detail or consistency is needed.
commonMisconceptions: Only checking spelling of the character's name rather than their development.
Thinking character development can't be checked or improved during editing.
hints: Think about consistency between what a character does and who they are.
A good question links the character's actions to their personality or feelings.

items.questionText: Which sentence is a question? A) The cat sat on the mat.   B) Where is the cat?   C) Sit down, please.
items.answerKey: Where is the cat?
stepByStepSolution: Think about the purpose of each sentence.
A question asks something and usually ends with a question mark.
'Where is the cat?' asks something, so it is a question.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any sentence with 'where' or 'what' is automatically a question, ignoring punctuation.
Confusing commands with questions.
hints: Look for the punctuation mark at the end of each sentence.
A question ends with a question mark.

items.questionText: Which sentence is a command? A) Please close the door.   B) The door is closed.   C) Is the door closed?
items.answerKey: Please close the door.
stepByStepSolution: Think about what each sentence is doing — telling, asking, or instructing.
A command gives an instruction or asks someone to do something.
'Please close the door' instructs someone to do an action, so it is a command.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking all polite sentences are statements, ignoring the instruction.
Confusing a statement about the door with an instruction to act.
